## **Chapter 2: Black bear habitat selection in response to wind energy**

## **Introduction**

In an era marked by a global shift towards renewable energy sources, wind energy has emerged as one of the fastest-growing sectors, second only to solar photovoltaic technologies (IEA, 2024). Onshore wind capacity specifically is expected to more than double in countries such as the United States, European Union, India, and Brazil by 2028 (IEA, 2024). However, the rapid growth of this sector has raised concerns regarding its potential impacts on wildlife. While much research has focused on the effects of wind energy development on volant species, particularly birds and bats (Pearce‐Higgins et al., 2009; Garvin et al., 2011; Marques et al., 2014; Thaxter et al., 2017; Guest et al., 2022), there is a growing interest in investigating the behavioural responses of terrestrial wildlife (Kuvlesky et al., 2007; Łopucki et al., 2017; Schöll & Nopp-Mayr, 2021; Tolvanen et al., 2023), because wind farms affect conditions both in the air and on the ground.

Wind farms have the potential to influence terrestrial animal behaviour through several mechanisms, one being fear. Animals often perceive human presence as increased predation risk, creating landscapes of fear (Laundré et al., 2001; Ciuti et al., 2012; Gaynor et al., 2019; Suraci et al., 2019). Increased human activity, such as that associated with wind farm construction and operation, can be a significant source of disturbance, particularly for sensitive animals (Helldin et al., 2012; da Costa & Alvares, 2018). Even without direct human presence, human developments such as wind turbines can emit sensory stimuli that provoke similar fear responses (Wilson et al., 2020). The rotation of the turbine blades creates a disturbance in terms of noise, visual effects, shadows, and vibrations, exerting variable changes in behaviour across a wide array of terrestrial species (Lovich & Ennen, 2013; Schöll & Nopp-Mayr, 2021; Tolvanen et al., 2023).

Behavioural responses often differ between the construction and operational phases of wind energy projects due to the varying nature and intensity of disturbance (Colman et al., 2012; Skarin & Alam, 2017). Animals might be more sensitive to wind farm disturbance during particular life history stages (Tsegaye et al., 2017; Skarin et al., 2018; Lloyd et al., 2022) or seasons (Eftestøl et al., 2023; Milligan et al., 2023). Animals must balance resource acquisition against avoiding danger (Gill et al., 1996), and these trade-offs can have direct fitness consequences. For example, increased vigilance often comes at the cost of reduced foraging

efficiency and overall energy intake (Laundré et al., 2001; Sweet et al., 2022). Additionally, animals can experience physiological stress in tandem with these fear-induced behaviours (Ditmer et al., 2015).

Beyond fear-based responses, wind energy developments also contribute to sensory pollution, particularly through noise and light, which can disrupt key behavioural processes. Modern industrial-scale wind turbines primarily emit sound at lower frequencies, with dominant energy below 1 kHz generated by blade turbulence and mechanical components (Møller & Pedersen, 2011). This low-frequency sound creates chronic acoustic disturbance, shown to interfere with communication between mothers and offspring (Skarin et al., 2018; Proett et al., 2022), reduce the ability of prey species to detect or alert others of predators (Rabin et al., 2006; Łopucki et al., 2017; Skarin et al., 2018; Proett et al., 2022) and disrupt reproductive displays (Winder et al., 2015; Zwart et al., 2015; Smith & Dwyer, 2016; LeBeau et al., 2017; Taubmann et al., 2021), resulting in fitness consequences. Additionally, low-frequency sound and infrasound may be perceived through somatosensory pathways as vibration or pressure fluctuations, a mechanism shown to elicit physiological and behavioural responses in humans (Leventhall, 2007). Wind energy developments can also alter natural light conditions (Bará & Lima, 2024), which can affect volant species (Jonasson et al., 2024) while the effect on terrestrial wildlife remains unexplored.

In addition to producing sensory disturbance, wind energy developments result in physical changes to landscape structure. The construction of wind farms results in direct habitat loss and fragmentation (Jones et al., 2015), potentially reducing habitat quality and resource availability near turbines (Colman et al., 2013; Campedelli et al., 2014; González et al., 2016; Coppes et al., 2020). Such structural changes might affect species interactions by changing the growing conditions for plants (Harris, 1984) and altering the accessibility of these areas to competitors and predators (May & Norton, 1996; Sirén et al., 2017). Increases in turbine-induced carrion can attract scavengers to wind farm sites (Villegas-Patraca et al., 2012; Tanis, 2014). The rotor action can also alter the microclimate in the vicinity of the operating turbines, potentially affecting vegetation productivity (McCallum et al., 2014; Armstrong et al., 2016; Rajewski et al., 2016).

Access roads built for wind energy infrastructure can directly affect wildlife (Colman et al., 2013; Taubmann et al., 2021). The broader ecological effects of roads on wildlife are well-

documented (Trombulak & Frissell, 2000), including their role in habitat fragmentation (Saunders et al., 2002), displacement from habitats (Northrup et al., 2012), and their capacity to act as barriers to movement and dispersal (Burnett, 1992; Alexander et al., 2005; Epps et al., 2005). Additionally, roads can increase the vulnerability to harvest by providing access to previously remote areas (Fa et al., 2005; Loosen et al., 2019; Proctor et al., 2019; Quintana et al., 2022).

Avoidance of wind energy developments is a common behavioural response among terrestrial wildlife. A recent review found that 61% of ground-dwelling birds and 67% of terrestrial mammals studied showed significant avoidance of wind turbine areas (Tolvanen et al., 2023). This avoidance was up to 5 km from wind turbines for ground-dwelling birds, 15 km for domestic reindeer ( _Rangifer tarandus tarandus_ ) in Sweden, and 0.7 km for smaller mammals such as red foxes ( _Vulpes vulpes_ ) and European hares ( _Lepus europaeus_ ) (Łopucki et al., 2017).

Another behavioural response to wind energy development is altered movement. Animals frequently adjust their movement patterns in response to perceived risk or disturbance. This might involve moving more quickly through high-risk areas (Wang et al., 2017) or taking longer, more circuitous routes to avoid them (Benson et al., 2021). For example, pronghorn antelope ( _Antilocapra americana_ ) were observed to increase travel speeds near turbines during the spring, and showed reduced fidelity to traditional migration routes that were near turbines under construction (Milligan et al., 2023). Such altered movements can increase energetic costs and reduce the animal’s ability to efficiently exploit available resources.

While altered habitat use and movement reflect spatial partitioning to avoid high-risk areas, animals might also engage in temporal partitioning (Kronfeld-Schor & Dayan, 2003), shifting their activity to times when perceived risk is lower. This can manifest as changes in daily activity patterns, such as increased nocturnality (Beckmann & Berger, 2003; Gaynor et al., 2018; Devarajan et al., 2025). Such shifts towards nocturnality might be particularly advantageous during the construction phase of wind energy projects, when human activity is largely restricted to daylight hours, allowing animals to reduce exposure to disturbance. While such daily temporal shifts have been observed in response to other types of human disturbance (Zeller et al., 2019), they remain largely unexplored in the context of wind energy development.

These local changes in habitat use, movement, and timing of activity can reduce access to resources (Houston et al., 2011). This phenomenon, known as functional habitat loss, occurs

when animals avoid otherwise suitable habitat due to perceived risk or disturbance. Human disturbance can generate functional habitat loss that greatly exceeds the spatial extent of the disturbance itself (Dyer et al., 2001; Whittington et al., 2005). These localised losses can scale up to landscape levels by altering patterns of distribution and movement (Tucker et al., 2018; Doherty et al., 2021). As animals are displaced from preferred habitats, they could be pushed into marginal areas or closer to human settlements or infrastructure, increasing the likelihood of human-wildlife conflict (Schuette et al., 2013). Lost foraging opportunities might drive individuals to seek alternative food sources in anthropogenic environments, further elevating conflict risk.

Although wind farms have relatively small physical footprints relative to other energy developments, they have the potential to evoke behavioural changes with considerable ecological consequences. Understanding these changes is useful for guiding future wind energy developments in ways that minimise impacts on wildlife. One species for which behavioural responses to wind energy developments remain unknown is the American black bear ( _Ursus americanus_ ). As the most widely distributed bear species in North America (Clark et al., 2020), black bears historically occupied most forested regions across the continent (Hall, 1981). However, expanding human land use has significantly reduced the quantity and quality of these habitats (Foley et al., 2005), often relegating bears to remote, rugged, or marginal areas that were previously unsuitable for human use (Pelton & van Manen, 1994). These same landscapes are now increasingly targeted for wind energy development (Hastik et al., 2015; Passoni et al., 2017; EEA, 2019). Given the growing spatial overlap between black bear habitat and areas suitable for wind energy development, it is critical to understand if and how wind farms influence black bear behaviour.

These behavioural changes could have ecological and social consequences. Black bears are adaptable and increasingly persist in fragmented forested areas near human development (Pelton, 2003). In these areas, the incidence of human-bear conflict is closely tied to natural food availability (Hellgren & Maehr, 1993; Howe et al., 2010; Baruch-Mordo et al., 2014; Obbard et al., 2014). When food is scarce, bears are more likely to travel beyond their usual home ranges in search of alternative resources (Matson, 1946; Eiler et al., 1989; Johnson et al., 2015; Price et al., 2024). Bears travelling through unfamiliar landscapes are more likely to intersect roads and experience an increased risk of vehicle collisions (Garshelis & Pelton, 1981; Rogers, 1987;

Brody & Pelton, 1989; Ryan et al., 2007; Wynn-Grant et al., 2018). Increased movement can also elevate bears' vulnerability to harvest, particularly when bears access open or predictable areas like corn fields, which are more easily targeted by hunters (Noyce & Garshelis, 1997; Kluge et al., 2024, VFWD, 2024). Bears may adopt the use of anthropogenic food sources, such as garbage, crops, fruit trees, or livestock, when these are encountered (Rogers, 1976; Johnson et al., 2015; Lewis et al., 2015; Ditmer et al., 2016). If wind turbines elicit spatial avoidance in bears, this can further reduce access to natural foraging areas, resulting in functional habitat loss. In turn, bears could be pushed into human areas – either to compensate for lost resources or simply as a consequence of being displaced – increasing the risk of conflict. Such conflicts are costly for both bears and people, often resulting in property damage, public safety concerns, and human-induced mortality for bears.

My research seeks to fill this knowledge gap by examining how American black bears respond to wind energy development. This case study centres on the construction and operation of the first commercial wind farm within a U.S. National Forest. The project site, located in the Green Mountain National Forest (GMNF) in southern Vermont, was built within one of the largest remaining contiguous tracts of high-quality black bear habitat in the state (VFWD, 2024). This habitat consists of mature American beech trees ( _Fagus grandifolia_ ). Beech trees produce beech nuts, an important source of fat and carbohydrates for bears in the fall as they prepare for hibernation (Elowe & Dodge, 1989; Servello & Kirkpatrick, 1989). Beech nuts ripen in the fall, aligning with bears’ hyperphagic period, during which they intensively forage to accumulate fat reserves for winter hibernation (Folk et al., 1976). Beech stands are highly selected habitats by bears in this area during many seasons (Dupuis et al., 2025), including in the spring, when bears forage on residual beech nuts from the previous fall (Hammond, 2002; McDonald & Fuller, 2005). These beech forests represent some of the area’s most valuable habitats for black bears, where few other hard mast species are present (Schooley, 1990; McDonald et al., 1994; Dupuis et al., 2025).

American beech exhibits a mast seeding pattern, producing highly variable beech nut crops from year to year (Kelly, 1994; Kelly & Sork, 2002). These fluctuations influence black bear movement, reproductive success, survival, and recruitment (Hugie, 1982; Elowe & Dodge, 1989; Hammond, 2002). Beech mast cycles can synchronise with bear reproductive patterns, through alternate-year cub production following high masting (Schooley, 1990; McLaughlin et

al., 1994; Jakubas et al., 2005). Bears exhibit strong site fidelity to beech stands during good mast years, often climbing mature trees to access nuts directly from the canopy. Repeated use of these trees over multiple years leaves visible claw marks on the bark of the trunks, allowing these bear-scarred beech trees to serve as evidence of long-term foraging activity (Wolfson & Hammond, 1992).

Recognising the importance of these habitats for black bears, the State of Vermont established legal protections for concentrated stands of bear-scarred beech trees by designating them as necessary wildlife habitat under its land use and development law, Act 250 (State of Vermont, 2024). These protections set a legal precedent under Act 250 and have been used to permit or modify many other proposed developments, including ski resorts, to avoid impacts to this important bear habitat (Hammond & Austin, 2011). Energy projects, including wind energy, are subject to Title 30 § 248 permitting, which incorporates many of the same concerns as Act 250, including protections for necessary wildlife habitat. Despite these legal precedents and concerns from State biologists, the GMNF wind energy project was granted a Certificate of Public Good (CPG) on April 16, 2009, and other required State permits to move forward without being required to avoid impacts to bear habitat. Instead, the Public Utility Commission required the project to file mitigation proposals in the form of bear habitat conservation and a study on the effects of wind development on black bear behaviour, including pre-construction, during construction, and post-construction monitoring.

My objective with this study was to evaluate whether the construction and operation of a commercial wind energy facility in high-quality black bear habitat influenced black bear behaviour. I addressed this objective by examining behavioural responses:

1. **Across development phases** (pre-construction, construction, post-construction), and, where effects were present, estimated the extent of avoidance and consequent functional habitat loss.

2. **Across seasons** , with a focus on the fall and spring of good beech mast years, when bears are most reliant on the habitats surrounding the wind farm, and disturbance effects were predicted to be strongest.

## 3. **At two spatial extents** :

- a. A **local** extent, close to turbines, where acute responses such as altered daily activity patterns, movement, and resource selection were predicted to occur. A

Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) design was used to determine whether these localised behavioural changes were directly attributable to wind farm activities.

b. A **landscape** extent, to assess broader patterns of habitat selection and potential increases in human-bear conflict risk. I predicted that local behaviour changes would scale up to influence landscape-level space use.

Findings from this study aim to inform the strategic planning of future wind energy projects by improving our understanding of black bear responses to wind energy development, minimising effects on wildlife while supporting the global transition to renewable energy.

## **Study Area**

The study area is centred around the 30-megawatt commercial wind energy facility built within the Manchester District of the Green Mountain National Forest (GMNF) in southern Vermont, U.S. The wind facility was built within a beech-dominated portion of the northern hardwood forest, which characterizes much of the GMNF (Figure 2.1). The facility consists of 15 wind turbines erected across 2 ridgelines in the towns of Searsburg and Readsboro. To support turbine installation and access, approximately 7 km of limited-access gravel roads were constructed to connect the 2 turbine strings via Vermont Route 8. The total project footprint, including turbines, road, and associated infrastructure, encompasses approximately 0.35 km[2] (86 acres). This footprint spans an elevational range of 734 to 947 m, with turbines at the highest points along each ridge and supporting infrastructure at slightly lower elevations. Site preparation required the clearing of approximately 360 mature American beech trees – 300 from the western ridge and 60 from the eastern ridge.

The broader study area extends into the northwestern corner of Massachusetts and eastern New York. This forested landscape supports high densities of black bears (New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, 2014; Massachusetts Division of Fisheries and Wildlife, 2023; VFWD, 2024), with fall hunting seasons active in all three states. Most of the landscape, both within the GMNF and outside, is predominantly forested with deciduous (38%) and mixed (31%) forest types, with evergreen forest representing only 8% of total land cover. These forested areas are often interspersed with soft mast species in forest canopy openings (Costello & Sage, 1994). Natural forest openings are uncommon due to the region’s humid continental climate, which limits the persistence of early successional habitat (Seymour, 1994).

Natural disturbance occurs from beaver-influenced wetlands, as well as infrequent wind and ice storm events. Early successional habitats also arise from modest timber harvest, totaling <1% of the GMNF forested area annually (USDA Forest Service, 2006). Most harvest occurs on privately owned lands outside of the GMNF (Butler et al., 2014) from small-scale anthropogenic disturbance. Human development, including roads, residences, energy infrastructure, and agriculture (hayfields, pasture, and cultivated crops), is present on roughly 15% of the area. Human population density is low throughout the study area, consisting mostly of rural communities and small towns, with larger population centres in the south and west.

## **Methods**

## Data Sources

Bear Location Data

The Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department deployed GPS radio-collars to track black bear locations and movement from 2012 through 2020. Capture efforts were concentrated within a 5-km radius of the future wind energy facility in southern Vermont (Appendix 5, Figure 1). Bear captures were conducted during the spring and summer, aiming to maintain a sample size of 12–15 individuals/year. New bears were added annually, with some individuals re-collared in multiple years. The primary capture method involved cable restraints (using the Aldrich Humane Foot Restraint and M-15 bucket designs), although trained bear hounds, barrel traps, and culvert traps were employed when appropriate. Bears were immobilized using Telazol (tiletamine hydrochloride and zolazepam hydrochloride), BAM (butorphanol, azaperone, and medetomidine), or TKX (Telazol, ketamine, and xylazine), administered via a syringe pole or dart rifle. Each bear was equipped with a GPS satellite collar, which included models from Lotek (Iridium and Litetrack Iridium, Lotek Wireless Inc., Newmarket, Ontario, Canada), Telonics (Mesa, Arizona, U.S.), or Vectronic (Vertex Plus, Vectronic Aerospace, Berlin, Germany). Collars were programmed to record GPS locations at 2-hour and 50-minute intervals.

GPS location data were screened to reduce positional error, with fixes exceeding a dilution of precision (DOP) value of 10 excluded from the analysis. Den entry and emergence dates were manually identified by inspecting GPS locations for each bear. GPS locations during the denning period were excluded to restrict the analysis to active movements. GPS locations recorded within 24 hours of collar deployment were also excluded to minimise potential bias

from capture-related disturbance. Additionally, data points clustered around active bait sites associated with the study were manually filtered out.

## Temporal Data

Bear location data were categorized by season and beech mast availability to capture variation in foraging behaviour. Following Hammond (2002), seasons were categorized as the following: spring as den emergence to June 15, summer as June 16 to August 31, and fall as September 1 until den entry. Seasons were further classified by beech mast availability, which represents the primary source of hard mast for black bears in the study area. Annual hard mast surveys were conducted by the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department (VFWD, unpublished) by counting nuts found beneath 20 randomly selected mature trees within designated monitoring survey stands. A season was classified as a good mast year if the average number of beech nuts per survey was ≥20, and a poor if <20. Red oak ( _Quercus rubra_ ) mast surveys were conducted concurrently using the same protocol and used to interpret habitat selection patterns, with good acorn production characterized as ≥200 acorns per survey, and poor as <200. Although primarily conducted in Vermont (some oak surveys occurred opportunistically in northwestern Massachusetts), these surveys likely reflect mast trends in the adjacent regions as mast synchrony has been observed over large distances (Koenig, 1999).

The cycle of beech seasons is as follows: beech nuts begin developing in the summer, marking the onset of a good summer. This is followed by a good fall when beech nuts ripen and reach peak availability, with bears foraging both in the canopy and on fallen nuts. A good spring follows a good fall, when bears might continue feeding on overwintered beech nuts that remain on the forest floor before they germinate. In contrast, a poor summer signifies no new beech crop is developing, leading to low or no beech availability in the poor fall and the poor spring that follow.

In addition to seasonal classification, data were grouped by construction phase. The preconstruction phase ran from the beginning of the study in 2012 until construction began in the fall of 2016. Construction continued until the end of 2017, followed by the post-construction (or operational) phase beginning in the spring of 2018. The operational phase continued until the end of 2020, when data collection ceased. Combining these classifications resulted in 16 temporal

categories: 6 beech seasons by 3 construction phases, as no construction occurred during a good spring or poor summer.

## Spatial Data

Habitat covariates used to explain selection patterns by bears were based on Dupuis et al. (2025), who examined seasonal patterns of habitat selection by bears in this study area before the construction of the wind farm. Final linear predictor covariates included percent basal area of beech, percent basal area of oak, distance to wetland, distance to open canopy, and developed density. All spatial processing was completed in ArcGIS Pro using the NAD 1983 UTM Zone 18N projection (Esri, 2024) with a pixel size of 10 x 10 meters. Beech and oak basal area layers were derived from spectral unmixing of Landsat imagery by Gudex-Cross et al. (2017), estimating the percentage of the total tree cross-sectional area (measured at breast height) represented by a given species within each pixel. Wetland features were identified using the National Wetlands Inventory (USFWS, 2022), and the distance from each pixel to the nearest wetland feature was calculated using GIS. Open canopies were used as a proxy for soft mast availability, an essential source of summer food for black bears in the northeastern U.S. (Garshelis & Pelton, 1981; Eagle & Pelton, 1983; Reynolds‐Hogland et al., 2007; Ryan et al., 2007). Open canopies were defined as pixels with 0-75% canopy cover from the USDA Forest Service’s Total Canopy Cover layer (2016). This threshold was determined through visual inspection to ensure biologically relevant classification, capturing open areas such as those beneath powerlines and windblown patches with known soft mast availability. Developed density was quantified using the 2016 National Land Cover Database (MLRC, 2016), summing pixels classified as either developed (all developed levels), cultivated crops, pasture, hay, or barren land within a 1-km[2] moving window. This scale was selected based on previous research demonstrating that a 1-km[2] area effectively captured how bears respond to nearby human development (Mace et al., 1996). Incorporating covariates at spatial scales that align with their ecological relevance can improve inferences in habitat selection analyses (Boyce et al., 2017).

The wind farm footprint was not included in the developed density footprint or as open canopy. However, in the beech mapping, the wind farm footprint was already categorized as non-forest with no beech. Because of the small extent of this footprint within both spatial extents

(1.52% of the local area and 0.006% of the landscape area), it was considered negligible in the analysis.

Collinearity among habitat covariates was assessed using Pearson’s correlation coefficient, with a threshold of _r_ = 0.7 for inclusion. The model selection process involved evaluating predictors both individually and in combination using Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) (Burnham & Anderson, 2004). I used the small-sample corrected version (AICc) to ensure consistency across models (Burnham et al., 2011). Covariates with low predictive power or negligible effect sizes were removed. Assumptions of linearity were confirmed for each covariate.

## Data Analyses

Landscape Extent

I used resource selection functions (RSFs) to evaluate changes in black bear habitat selection relative to availability (Manly et al., 2002). I estimated population-level changes in habitat selection to support generalizable recommendations for wind energy development by employing a Design 1 sampling approach, generating availability from a consistent study area for all bears (Manly et al., 2002). This study area was defined by creating a polygon encompassing all bear locations across all years. Measuring roughly 70 km by 100 km, the area was considered realistically available to bears given their high mobility and the multi-year duration of this study. Due to incomplete forest mapping, the southeastern corner of the study area polygon was excluded from analyses (0.97% of locations removed). To measure habitat selection, I generated a used-available dataset in the R package _amt_ (Signer et al., 2019). For every used location (coded as 1), ten random available locations (coded as 0) were sampled within the defined study area. Spatial attributes were extracted from the 10-by-10-meter pixels at all used and available locations, which served as the resource units for the analysis.
